newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russia seeks big cuts in new budget plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia seeks big cuts in new budget plan.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, pressing ahead with unpopular economic policies, urged parliament on Wednesday to back plans to slash spending across the board.

Chernomyrdin, reviewing the Russian economy in the first quarter of this year, said there were signs of growth in several sectors. Budget revenues had improved in March and April, but spending was still too high.

"The situation in March and April has improved somewhat, but this is still not conclusive," Chernomyrdin told the State Duma lower house of parliament. "We have no reason to hope that the situation will improve by itself."
Under a budget law passed last year, the Duma must approve new spending levels if revenue is more than 10 percent below plan.

But the government has already cut spending and President Boris Yeltsin, in a clear snub to the conservative dominated Duma, summoned Chernomyrdin and other ministers to the Kremlin in the middle of the debate.
The Kremlin gave no reason for the summons, but Itar-Tass news agency said the president wanted his most senior ministers to attend a ceremony honouring cellist Mstislav Rostropovich.
Chernomyrdin left the chamber but stayed in the building and First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, the main architect of the reform programme, returned after a brief interval.

Chubais, the mastermind of Russia's privatisation programme, is a figure of hate for the communists and their allies and Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov on Wednesday urged Yeltsin to rethink his government line-up.

"The government is made up of people personally responsible for policies hostile to the population -- impoverishment and rip-off privatisation. We must suggest that the president reviews the cabinet," Zyuganov told deputies.
"We must recognise the work of the cabinet as unsatisfactory, noting that the under-achievement of the budget is a result of Yeltsin's vicious policy."

Even the small group of liberals in the parliament is bitter at government action and Grigory Yavlinsky, who heads the Duma's Yabloko group, told reporters he had collected 93 signatures calling for a vote of no-confidence in the government.

Under Duma rules, such a vote must be put on the agenda within seven days if more than 90 deputies call for it but most deputies, including the communists, have indicated they do not want to topple the government.
Chernomyrdin's calls for spending cuts are due to dismal tax collection and poor budget discipline, which have created a web of non-payments and left millions below the poverty line.

Some communist deputies want to double the money supply to provide companies and the government with the cash they need to pay overdue bills, but Chernomyrdin said the government would never agree to this.
"The government and above all the central bank are carrying out a policy to control monetary emission which is aimed at lowering interest rates," he said.
The prime minister said a large increase in money supply would re-ignite inflation, widen the budget deficit and cause the rouble to crash.

Consumer prices are expected to rise 12 percent this year, just over half the level seen in 1996. Economic output is expected to stay flat although some sectors -- notably machine building, oil and light industry -- are already growing.

Chernomyrdin, noting that the government was being open about its plans to cut spending, said the government had over-estimated its ability to collect taxes and now needed to sequester funds. It also needed to cut spending for all but essential services.
He said revenues in the first four months of this year were only 64.6 percent of budgeted levels, while expenditure was curtailed to 70 percent of that planned for the period.
The government now wants to cut 108 trillion roubles from spending levels outlined in the "unrealistic" 1997 budget. Deputies are due to vote on the proposal on Friday.
